input:
In this study, the adsorption of a dye from water onto activated carbon was investigated in a series of batch tests carried out at 298 K. The experimental data were fitted to the Langmuir model, giving a fitted capacity of 257 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7, which represents the maximum monolayer loading predicted by the model under these conditions. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, the removal achieved after 120 min was 85% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, corresponding to a residual concentration of 7.5 mg L-1 remaining in solution.

It is important to understand that the capacity of 257 mg per gram is a parameter obtained from the fit rather than a directly measured loading. Essentially, it is the plateau that the Langmuir equation assigns to the isotherm at pH 7, and it therefore describes the carbon and dye combination at that specific pH value only. The capacity at other pH values was not measured, and the figure should not be assumed to transfer across pH, since the charge carried by the dye and by the carbon surface both vary with pH, and the fitted value inevitably absorbs the combined effect of these changes.

Similarly, the removal figure of 85% is tied to the particular conditions under which it was obtained. With a dose of 0.6 g L-1 and an initial concentration of 50 mg L-1, a total of 42.5 mg L-1 was removed over the course of 120 min, and a different dose or a different starting concentration would produce a different percentage removal without any change in the carbon itself. The 85% figure can therefore only really be used to rank this carbon against other carbons when the comparison is made at the same dose, the same initial concentration, and the same contact time.
target:
Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon, measured in batch tests at 298 K, fitted a Langmuir capacity of 257 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 85% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, leaving 7.5 mg L-1 in solution.

The capacity figure is a fit parameter, not a measured loading: it is the plateau the Langmuir equation assigns to the isotherm at pH 7, and it describes the carbon-dye pair at that pH only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured, and the value does not transfer across pH, because the charge on the dye and on the carbon surface both move with pH and the fit absorbs their combined effect.

The fitted capacity also fixes the scale of the removal test. A capacity of 257 mg per gram is the loading the carbon carries at the plateau of the isotherm, well above the loading reached in a test that removes 85% of the dye in solution, and the two figures describe different regions of the same isotherm: the removal test works on its rising part, where sites are still free, and states nothing about the plateau the fit extrapolates.

The removal figure belongs to its conditions. A dose of 0.6 g L-1 against an initial concentration of 50 mg L-1 removed 42.5 mg L-1 in 120 min; a weaker solution or a larger dose changes the percentage without any change in the carbon. The 85% ranks this carbon against others only at the same dose, concentration, and contact time.
